titre: Thirteen Trillion Zeros Checked, Still No Proof
accroche: In 1859, Riemann notes in passing that some zeros are, in his words, “very probably” all aligned. No one has been able to prove it since.
contenu_vulgarise:
In November 1859, Bernhard Riemann publishes the only paper he will ever write on prime numbers, in the proceedings of the Berlin Academy of Sciences. Prime numbers follow no simple rule (no one can predict the next one), yet Riemann shows that one can still count, with precision, how many there are below a given threshold, provided one understands the behavior of a function he studies, the zeta function, originally defined as an infinite sum and extended by Riemann to almost every complex number.

## A Remark Tossed Off in Passing

This function vanishes at infinitely many points. Some of these zeros, called “trivial,” are easy to spot and hold no interest for prime numbers. The others, the non-trivial zeros, are the ones that matter: the more precisely their position is known, the more accurate Riemann's formula for counting primes becomes. Riemann notes that every non-trivial zero he has been able to compute shares the same real part, 1/2: they line up on what will come to be called the “critical line.” He then writes, without dwelling on it: “Es ist sehr wahrscheinlich, dass alle Wurzeln reell sind,” that is, it is very probable that all roots are real. He does not prove it, notes that doing so does not seem necessary for his immediate purpose, and moves on.

That one-line, unproven remark will become the Riemann hypothesis: one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems, announced on May 24, 2000, by the Clay Mathematics Institute, each carrying a million-dollar reward for whoever solves it. Only one of the seven has been solved since, the Poincaré conjecture, by Grigori Perelman, who turned the prize down in 2010. The other six, including Riemann's, still stand.

## Why Billions of Checks Are Not Enough

The hypothesis has been tested, one by one, on more than thirteen trillion zeros, without a single one ever straying from the critical line. One might think this amounts to proof in practice. It is the opposite of what these calculations teach mathematicians, and the story of Skewes' number explains why. In the early twentieth century, it was believed that the number of primes below a given threshold always stayed below a theoretical estimate, the logarithmic integral, an observation confirmed on every case that could be computed by hand. In 1914, John Littlewood proved that this pattern eventually reverses, infinitely many times in fact, without saying where. His successor Stanley Skewes calculated, in 1933 and again in 1955, bounds where this reversal must necessarily occur: numbers so large, on the order of a tower of three exponentials, that no exhaustive search will ever reach them one by one.

The first actual reversal in fact sits much lower, near 1.4 × 10³¹⁶. The point lies elsewhere: a rule true for billions, even trillions of cases, can still collapse beyond them. That is why, in mathematics, checking is never the same as proving, and why the Riemann hypothesis, confirmed on thirteen trillion zeros, remains, a hundred and sixty-seven years after that remark tossed off in 1859, a hypothesis.

carte.punch: Riemann notes that some zeros are “very probably” aligned. No one has proven it since.
carte.idee: In 1859, Riemann tosses off an unproven remark about the zeros of his zeta function: they would all be aligned on a single line. Verified on thirteen trillion cases without exception, the hypothesis is worth a million dollars to whoever proves it. No one has managed to in a hundred and sixty-seven years.

quiz.question: Why don't mathematicians consider the Riemann hypothesis as good as proven, despite thirteen trillion checks without a single exception?
choix: Because the checks actually found several counterexamples that were never published
Because a pattern true for an extremely large number of cases can still reverse beyond them, as shown by Skewes' number for prime numbers
Because the zeta function is only defined for real numbers, which limits what the checks can cover
Because the Clay Mathematics Institute requires a proof written by hand, without a computer
quiz.explication: Skewes' number shows that a pattern confirmed on an enormous number of cases (here, π(x) < li(x)) can still reverse beyond the reach of any possible check; the zeros verified so far cover only a bounded range, and nothing guarantees the critical line holds beyond it.
